title: Spider-Like Harvestmen Reveal How Parental Care Evolved — Thanks to Citizen Scientists
hook: Photos uploaded by amateur naturalists just solved a long-standing puzzle about how fatherhood evolved in one strange arachnid group.
key_points: Harvestmen (spider-like arachnids, not true spiders) show unusually varied parental care — some species guard eggs as mothers, others as fathers.
Researchers mined thousands of public photos and observations from the citizen-science platform iNaturalist to study this at a scale no single lab study could match.
The project more than doubled the known cases of egg-guarding behavior in harvestmen, completed in just days using crowdsourced data.
Maternal and paternal care turned out to have followed different evolutionary paths, rather than one simply being a variant of the other.
The study doubles as a case study in citizen science's growing power to answer questions that would otherwise take years of fieldwork.
content_html: Harvestmen — leggy arachnids often mistaken for spiders — turn out to be unusually flexible about who does the parenting: in some species mothers guard the eggs, in others it's the fathers. Figuring out how that split evolved took an unlikely research team: thousands of amateur nature photographers.
extra_html: Researchers mined the citizen-science platform iNaturalist for photos and field notes of harvestmen guarding eggs, more than doubling the number of documented egg-guarding cases in a matter of days — a scale of data collection that would have taken a conventional field study years to match. Sorting through those observations revealed that maternal and paternal egg-guarding didn't evolve as two versions of the same behavior; they followed distinct evolutionary paths, arising independently in different lineages. Beyond the harvestmen result itself, the project is a demonstration of how crowdsourced, publicly contributed data can answer evolutionary questions that professional fieldwork alone struggles to resolve.

related.title: Natural Selection
related.hook: No designer, no goal — just heritable variation, a struggle to survive, and the slow accumulation of whatever happens to work. That's how life adapts.

related.title: How Animals Behave
related.hook: A spider spins a perfect web without a lesson, while a crow figures out a new trick by trial and error — two sides of how animals act in the world.
